title: War and Climate
gist: Six months into the Iran war, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is still destabilizing the global economy; Muggah, Nobre and Rockstrom argue the conflict is also pushing governments toward coal and biofuels, which will accelerate deforestation, raise CO2 emissions and undermine climate negotiations long after the fighting ends.

themes.theme: Hormuz as a persistent energy shock

insights.claim: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated how quickly a regional conflict can throw global energy markets into chaos, and six months into the Iran war the standoff continues to rattle the global economy.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: A chokepoint disruption has persisted for six months rather than mean-reverting, arguing for a structurally higher energy-risk premium than short-shock models assume.
insights.quote: Six months into the Iran war, the standoff in the Strait of Hormuz continues to rattle the global economy.
insights.locator: RIO DE JANEIRO—Six months into the Iran war

insights.claim: Traders and governments are watching for signs of escalation while households and companies pay more for fuel and fear energy shortages, keeping both a price and a physical-availability premium in the market.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: Two distinct risk channels to hedge: price via energy futures and volume via shortage-exposed industrials and utilities.
insights.quote: Traders and governments are watching for signs of escalation, while households and companies are paying more for fuel and fearing energy shortages.
insights.locator: Traders and governments are watching for signs of escalation

insights.claim: The war is pushing governments toward coal and biofuels as substitutes for disrupted oil supply, reversing the direction of energy-transition policy under security pressure.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: Security-driven fuel substitution is a demand tailwind for coal and biofuel producers and a headwind for transition-linked policy assets and carbon pricing.
insights.quote: By pushing governments toward coal and biofuels, the war could accelerate deforestation and undermine climate negotiations
insights.locator: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz showed how quickly

insights.claim: The shift to biofuels could accelerate deforestation, creating a land-use and ecological cost channel distinct from the direct emissions of burning fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: Watch agricultural land conversion and associated commodity supply in biofuel feedstock regions; also a rising ESG and regulatory exposure for biofuel supply chains.
insights.locator: By pushing governments toward coal and biofuels

insights.claim: The war is driving up carbon dioxide emissions and undermining international cooperation on climate change, a deeper and less visible toll than the visible energy-price shock.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: Implies weaker global climate policy momentum — relevant to carbon-price expectations and to the policy support underpinning clean-energy valuations.
insights.quote: the war is also taking a deeper, albeit less visible, environmental toll, driving up carbon dioxide emissions and undermining international cooperation on climate change
insights.locator: But the war is also taking a deeper

insights.claim: Unlike high oil prices, the environmental and climate-cooperation costs of the war will not disappear when the fighting ends, making them structural rather than cyclical.
insights.speaker: Robert Muggah
insights.so_what: Separates the mean-reverting trade (oil price) from the permanent one (climate policy setback) — the second is where positioning should be longer-dated.
insights.quote: And unlike high oil prices, those costs will not disappear when the war ends.
